label: First Ford Automobile -- Assembled in Detroit
summary: In June 1896 Henry Ford test-drove his Quadricycle, a light frame on four bicycle wheels with a two-cylinder ethanol engine, through the streets of Detroit. The same year Charles Dow began publishing his Industrial Average of 12 stocks, dominated by commodity businesses such as cotton oil, sugar and leather.

label: Boston First Subway / Klondike Gold Rush
summary: Boston opened the Tremont Street Subway in September 1897, the first subway in the United States. Months earlier, ships carrying Yukon gold reached Seattle and San Francisco and set off the Klondike Gold Rush, sending some 100,000 prospectors north and adding to the gold supply after years of depression following the Panic of 1893.

label: The Spanish American War
summary: After the USS Maine exploded in Havana harbor, the United States went to war with Spain. The fighting lasted about ten weeks. Under the Treaty of Paris the U.S. gained Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines, and Cuba won independence from Spain. The quick victory marked America's arrival as an overseas power.

label: First Hague Conference
summary: Twenty-six nations met at The Hague at the invitation of Tsar Nicholas II to discuss disarmament and the laws of war. The conference produced conventions on the conduct of land warfare and created the Permanent Court of Arbitration, an early attempt to settle disputes between countries without war.

label: Congress Establishes the Gold Standard
summary: The Gold Standard Act of March 1900 fixed the dollar at 25.8 grains of 90% gold and ended the long political fight over free silver. Pegging the currency to gold gave investors and foreign lenders confidence that the dollar would hold its value, though it also tied the money supply to gold discoveries.

label: McKinley Shot, T. Roosevelt becomes President
summary: President William McKinley was shot by an anarchist at the Pan-American Exposition in Buffalo and died eight days later. Theodore Roosevelt, 42, became the youngest president. The same year a fight for control of the Northern Pacific Railroad caused the Panic of May 1901, the first crash on the New York Stock Exchange.

label: Isthmian Canal Act -- Authorizes Panama Canal
summary: The Spooner Act authorized President Roosevelt to buy the rights and assets of the failed French canal company in Panama, then a province of Colombia, for $40 million. After Colombia refused the treaty terms, Panama declared independence in 1903 with U.S. support, and construction began in 1904.

label: Wright Brothers -- First Powered Flights
summary: On December 17, 1903, at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, Orville and Wilbur Wright made four controlled, powered flights. The longest covered 852 feet in 59 seconds. In markets, 1903 brought the so-called Rich Man's Panic, as overextended trusts and railroads fell and the Dow lost nearly a quarter of its value.

label: Russo-Japanese War
summary: Japan attacked the Russian fleet at Port Arthur in February 1904 over rival claims to Manchuria and Korea. Japan's victories on land and its destruction of the Russian Baltic Fleet at Tsushima in 1905 shocked Europe. Theodore Roosevelt brokered the peace treaty and won the Nobel Peace Prize for it.

label: Life Insurance Scandals -- Reform Legislation
summary: A dispute inside the Equitable Life Assurance Society exposed lavish spending of policyholder money. New York's Armstrong Committee, with Charles Evans Hughes as counsel, investigated the big insurers and found political payoffs and speculation. The resulting laws limited how insurers could invest and became a model for regulation across the country.

label: San Francisco Earthquake
summary: On April 18, 1906, a magnitude 7.9 earthquake and the fires that followed destroyed most of San Francisco and killed about 3,000 people. Insurance payouts drained gold from London and New York to California, tightening credit worldwide. The Dow peaked in January 1906 at a level it would not sustainably regain for about 19 years.

label: Financial Panic / Stock Market Crash
summary: A failed attempt to corner the stock of United Copper triggered runs on New York trust companies, starting with the Knickerbocker Trust. With no central bank, J.P. Morgan organized bankers to pump money into the system. The Dow fell about 49% from its 1906 peak, and the crisis led directly to the creation of the Federal Reserve.

label: Model T Ford is Introduced
summary: Ford introduced the Model T in October 1908 at $850. With the moving assembly line from 1913, the price fell below $300 by the 1920s, and about 15 million were built. The car changed where Americans lived and worked. Congress also passed the Aldrich-Vreeland Act in 1908 to provide emergency currency after the 1907 panic.

label: Admiral Robert E. Peary -- Reaches the North Pole
summary: Robert Peary, with Matthew Henson and four Inuit companions, announced that he reached the North Pole on April 6, 1909. His claim was disputed at the time by Frederick Cook and later questioned by historians who doubt his navigation. The Dow finished the year near 99, recovering most of the 1907 losses.

label: Democrats Control House -- First Time Since 1894
summary: In the 1910 midterm elections, voters frustrated with rising prices and the Payne-Aldrich Tariff gave Democrats control of the House of Representatives for the first time since 1894. The split between Taft's conservatives and Roosevelt's progressives inside the Republican Party set up the three-way presidential race of 1912.

label: Supreme Court -- Orders Standard Oil Co. Dissolved
summary: In Standard Oil Co. of New Jersey v. United States, the Supreme Court ruled that John D. Rockefeller's company was an illegal monopoly under the Sherman Antitrust Act and ordered it broken into 34 companies. Descendants include ExxonMobil and Chevron. Shareholders who kept the pieces ended up wealthier than before.

label: Titanic Sinks
summary: The RMS Titanic struck an iceberg on its maiden voyage and sank on April 15, 1912, killing more than 1,500 people. The disaster led to the first International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea, which required enough lifeboats for everyone aboard and round-the-clock radio watches.

label: First Income Tax -- 16th Amendment
summary: The 16th Amendment, ratified in February 1913, allowed Congress to tax income without dividing it among the states by population. The first modern income tax that year had a top rate of 7%. In December Congress also passed the Federal Reserve Act, creating the central bank the 1907 panic had shown was missing.

label: WW I -- in Europe / Federal Reserve Organized
summary: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in June led to war across Europe by August. Fearing a wave of European selling, the New York Stock Exchange closed from July 31 to December 12, 1914, its longest shutdown ever. The twelve Federal Reserve Banks opened in November.

label: Lusitania -- Sunk by German Submarine
summary: A German U-boat torpedoed the British liner Lusitania off Ireland on May 7, 1915, killing 1,198 people, including 128 Americans. Public anger in the U.S. grew, but the country stayed neutral. War orders from Europe drove a boom in American industry, and 1915 was one of the Dow's best years ever, up about 82%.

label: Emergency Revenue Act -- Includes Estate Tax
summary: To pay for military preparedness, the Revenue Act of 1916 raised the top income tax rate to 15% and created the modern federal estate tax, along with a tax on munitions profits. The Dow was also changed this year from 12 to 20 stocks, which is why the chart's early values are not perfectly continuous.

label: U.S. Formally Declares War on Germany
summary: After Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare and the Zimmermann Telegram proposed a German alliance with Mexico, Congress declared war on April 6, 1917. Liberty Bonds financed the effort, and taxes rose steeply. The Dow fell about 22% that year as investors weighed war costs and price controls.

label: World War I -- Ends / Daylight Savings Time
summary: The armistice of November 11, 1918, ended the fighting in World War I. Earlier that year the Standard Time Act introduced daylight saving time in the U.S. to save fuel. The 1918 influenza pandemic, which killed about 675,000 Americans, swept the country in the same months.

label: 18th Amendment, Prohibition -- Ratified
summary: The 18th Amendment banning the manufacture and sale of alcohol was ratified in January 1919 and took effect a year later. Prohibition wiped out a large legal industry and created a profitable criminal one. Markets enjoyed a short postwar boom in 1919 before a sharp recession followed.

label: 19th Amendment, Women's Suffrage -- Ratified
summary: Tennessee's ratification in August 1920 made the 19th Amendment law and guaranteed women the right to vote. The same year brought the Depression of 1920 to 1921, a short, severe slump with steep deflation as the Fed raised interest rates. The Dow fell about 33% in 1920.

label: The First Restrictive Immigration Act
summary: The Emergency Quota Act limited yearly immigration from each country to 3% of the people from that country living in the U.S. in 1910. It sharply reduced arrivals from Southern and Eastern Europe. The Dow hit its low near 64 in August 1921 and then began the long climb of the 1920s.

label: Federal Narcotics Control Board -- "War on Drugs"
summary: The Narcotic Drugs Import and Export Act of 1922 created the Federal Narcotics Control Board to regulate imports of opium and coca. Together with the earlier Harrison Act, it marked the start of federal drug enforcement. The economy recovered strongly, and the Dow rose about 22%.

label: First Transcontinental Flight / Japan Earthquake
summary: In May 1923 Army pilots John Macready and Oakley Kelly flew a Fokker T-2 nonstop from New York to San Diego in under 27 hours. In September the Great Kanto earthquake destroyed much of Tokyo and Yokohama and killed more than 100,000 people. President Harding died in August, and Calvin Coolidge took office.

label: Ford Manufactures 10 Millionth Automobile
summary: Ford's 10 millionth car, a Model T, left the line in June 1924. About half the cars on the road worldwide were Fords. Mass production and installment credit were remaking consumer spending. The Dow rose about 26% in 1924 and climbed past its 1906 peak for good.

label: "Scopes Monkey Trial"
summary: Tennessee teacher John Scopes was tried for teaching evolution in violation of state law. Clarence Darrow defended him and William Jennings Bryan helped prosecute. Scopes was convicted and fined $100, though the verdict was overturned on a technicality. The bull market gathered speed, and the Dow gained about 30%.

label: Revenue Act -- Reduces Income & Estate Taxes
summary: Treasury Secretary Andrew Mellon pushed through the Revenue Act of 1926, which cut the top income tax rate to 25% and halved the estate tax. A collapse of the Florida land boom that year was an early warning about speculative excess. The Dow ended 1926 roughly flat.

label: Lindbergh - First Nonstop Flight - New York to Paris
summary: Charles Lindbergh flew the Spirit of St. Louis solo from Long Island to Paris in 33.5 hours in May 1927 and became a global celebrity. Aviation stocks soared in the excitement. The Fed lowered interest rates that summer, and the Dow rose about 29%.

label: Amelia Earhart -- First Woman to Fly Atlantic
summary: Amelia Earhart crossed the Atlantic as a passenger in June 1928, becoming the first woman to do so by air. She flew it solo in 1932. In 1928 the Dow was expanded to 30 stocks and rose about 48% as buying on margin, with as little as 10% down, spread to ordinary investors.

label: Financial Panic -- Stock Market Crash -- Depression
summary: The Dow peaked at 381.17 on September 3, 1929. Selling turned to panic on Black Thursday, October 24, and on October 28 and 29 the Dow lost about 23% in two days. The crash wiped out margin buyers and shook confidence in banks. It was the start of a fall of almost 90% over the next three years.

label: Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act
summary: Despite a petition from more than 1,000 economists, President Hoover signed the Smoot-Hawley Tariff in June 1930, raising duties on over 20,000 imported goods. Other countries retaliated, and world trade fell by about two thirds over the next few years. A spring rally in stocks failed, and the Dow lost about 34% in 1930.

label: Bank Panic -- Country-Wide Bank Closings
summary: Waves of bank runs closed more than 2,000 U.S. banks in 1931. Austria's Creditanstalt failed in May, and Britain left the gold standard in September. The Fed raised interest rates to defend the dollar, deepening the slump. The Dow fell about 53% in 1931, its worst calendar year on record.

label: Lindbergh Kidnapping / Reconstruction Finance Corp.
summary: The kidnapping and murder of Charles Lindbergh's infant son shocked the nation. Congress created the Reconstruction Finance Corporation to lend to banks and railroads. The Dow hit bottom at 41.22 on July 8, 1932, down 89% from its 1929 peak. Unemployment reached about 24%, and Franklin Roosevelt won the presidency in November.

label: The New Deal -- Begins / FDIC Established
summary: Roosevelt took office in March, declared a national bank holiday, and in his first hundred days signed laws on banking, farms, industry and relief. The Glass-Steagall Act created the FDIC to insure deposits, which ended the bank runs. The U.S. left the gold standard, and the Dow rose about 67%, one of its best years.

label: Securities & Exchange Commission -- Established
summary: The Securities Exchange Act of 1934 created the SEC to regulate stock exchanges, require regular company reports and police fraud and manipulation. Joseph Kennedy, a former market speculator, was its first chairman. The Gold Reserve Act revalued gold from $20.67 to $35 an ounce.

label: Social Security Act -- Passed
summary: The Social Security Act created federal old-age pensions funded by payroll taxes, along with unemployment insurance and aid to dependent children. The Wagner Act guaranteed workers' right to unionize. Recovery was gaining ground, and the Dow climbed about 39%.

label: Drought in Western States -- "Dust Bowl"
summary: Severe drought and decades of plowing up native grassland turned the southern Plains into the Dust Bowl, with dust storms that blacked out the sky. Hundreds of thousands of families left for California and elsewhere. Industrial recovery continued, and the Dow rose about 25% to finish near 180.

label: Hindenburg -- Destroyed
summary: The German airship Hindenburg caught fire while docking at Lakehurst, New Jersey, in May 1937, killing 36 people and ending the era of passenger airships. That year the government cut spending and the Fed doubled bank reserve requirements, causing the Recession of 1937 to 1938. The Dow fell about 33%.

label: The New Deal -- Ends / Fair Labor Standards Act
summary: The Fair Labor Standards Act set the first federal minimum wage at 25 cents an hour, a 44-hour work week and limits on child labor. It was the last major New Deal law, as Republicans gained in the midterms. Former NYSE president Richard Whitney went to prison for embezzlement, which strengthened the SEC's hand.

label: World War II -- Begins in Europe / Great Depression
summary: Germany invaded Poland on September 1, 1939, and Britain and France declared war. The U.S. stayed neutral but in November allowed arms sales to the Allies on a cash-and-carry basis. Unemployment was still about 17%. Stocks jumped briefly on the war news, but the Dow ended the year slightly lower.

label: France Falls -- German Occupation
summary: Germany overran the Netherlands, Belgium and France in six weeks in the spring of 1940. Britain evacuated its army from Dunkirk and fought the Battle of Britain alone. The Dow fell sharply in May. Congress passed the first peacetime draft and the Investment Company Act regulating mutual funds.

label: Pearl Harbor -- Attacked by Japanese
summary: Japan attacked the U.S. Pacific Fleet at Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941, killing about 2,400 Americans. The U.S. declared war on Japan the next day, and Germany declared war on the U.S. days later. Earlier, Lend-Lease had begun supplying Britain. The Dow fell about 15% in 1941.

label: Price Controls -- Begin / Battle of Midway / Guadalcanal
summary: The Office of Price Administration froze most prices and began rationing sugar, gasoline and other goods. In June the U.S. Navy sank four Japanese carriers at Midway, turning the war in the Pacific, and in August Marines landed on Guadalcanal. The Dow bottomed near 93 in April 1942 and rallied for the rest of the war.

label: Current Tax Payment Act, Withholding Taxes
summary: The Current Tax Payment Act required employers to withhold income tax from paychecks, so taxes were paid as income was earned. With most workers now paying income tax, withholding made collection practical. Allied forces won in North Africa and invaded Italy, and the Dow gained about 14%.

label: Normandy Invasion
summary: On D-Day, June 6, 1944, Allied forces landed on the beaches of Normandy in the largest seaborne invasion in history, and Paris was freed in August. In July the Bretton Woods conference created the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank and tied world currencies to the dollar. The GI Bill was signed.

label: World War II -- Ends / Cold War -- Begins
summary: Germany surrendered in May 1945. After atomic bombs destroyed Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August, Japan surrendered. The United Nations was founded, and tensions with the Soviet Union over Eastern Europe began the Cold War. Roosevelt died in April and Harry Truman became president. The Dow rose about 27%.

label: Stock Market Crash / Price Controls -- End
summary: As wartime price controls ended, prices rose about 18% within a year and a wave of strikes followed. Investors feared a postwar depression like 1920, and the Dow fell about 23% from its May peak by the fall. Instead, the economy absorbed millions of returning veterans without a slump.

label: Taft-Hartley Act / Marshall Plan
summary: Over Truman's veto, Congress passed the Taft-Hartley Act, which limited union power by banning closed shops and secondary boycotts. Secretary of State George Marshall proposed a plan to rebuild Europe that would send about $13 billion in aid. The Truman Doctrine pledged U.S. support against communist pressure.

label: Truman Upsets Dewey -- For Presidency
summary: Nearly every poll and newspaper predicted Thomas Dewey would win, and the Chicago Tribune printed "Dewey Defeats Truman" on election night. Truman won. Stocks fell on the surprise, and the Dow ended the year about where it started. The Soviet blockade of Berlin led to the Berlin Airlift.

label: Foreign Currencies Devalued
summary: In September 1949 Britain devalued the pound by 30%, from $4.03 to $2.80, and more than 20 countries followed. The Soviet Union tested its first atomic bomb, NATO was formed, and communists took control of China. A mild recession ended in the fall, and the Dow began a bull market that lasted most of the 1950s.

label: The Korean War -- Begins
summary: North Korea invaded South Korea in June 1950, and U.S. troops led a United Nations force to defend it. Stocks fell about 12% on the news but recovered as defense spending rose. The Dow ended 1950 up about 18%.

label: First Commercial Color TV Broadcast
summary: CBS aired the first commercial color television broadcast in June 1951, using a system incompatible with existing black-and-white sets, and the service was soon halted. The Treasury-Fed Accord freed the Federal Reserve from holding down interest rates on government debt, which restored its independence.

label: Steel Workers Strike -- Despite Government Intervention
summary: To head off a strike during the Korean War, President Truman seized the steel mills. In Youngstown Sheet & Tube v. Sawyer the Supreme Court ruled the seizure unconstitutional, and 560,000 steelworkers struck for 53 days. Dwight Eisenhower won the presidency in November, and the Dow rose about 8%.

label: The Korean War -- Ends / Wage & Salary Controls End
summary: An armistice signed in July 1953 ended the fighting in Korea, and Eisenhower ended the remaining wage and price controls. Joseph Stalin died in March. Lower defense spending caused a mild recession, and the Dow slipped about 4%.

label: St. Lawrence Seaway Bill -- Passed
summary: Congress authorized the St. Lawrence Seaway, a joint project with Canada to let ocean ships sail into the Great Lakes. In November 1954 the Dow closed above its 1929 peak of 381 for the first time, 25 years after the crash. It rose about 44% that year. Brown v. Board of Education ended legal school segregation.

label: President Eisenhower -- Suffers a Heart Attack
summary: Eisenhower had a heart attack in September 1955. The next trading day the Dow fell 6.5%, its biggest one-day drop since 1929, as investors worried about his health and a reelection run. He recovered and won a second term in 1956. The AFL and CIO merged, and the Dow ended 1955 up about 21%.

label: Suez Canal -- Crisis
summary: Egypt's President Nasser nationalized the Suez Canal in July 1956. Britain, France and Israel invaded, but pressure from the U.S. and the Soviet Union forced them to withdraw. The crisis marked the end of Britain as a leading world power. The Soviet Union crushed the Hungarian uprising, and the Dow ended about flat.

label: Sputnik I
summary: The Soviet Union launched Sputnik, the first artificial satellite, in October 1957. Americans worried that they had fallen behind in science and missiles, and the government soon put more money into science education. The economy slipped into the Eisenhower recession, and the Dow fell about 13%.

label: U.S. -- First Satellite Launched
summary: Explorer 1 reached orbit in January 1958 and discovered the Van Allen radiation belts. Congress created NASA that summer, and the National Defense Education Act funded science and language studies. The recession ended in April, and the Dow rose about 34%.

label: St. Lawrence Seaway -- Opened
summary: Queen Elizabeth II and President Eisenhower opened the St. Lawrence Seaway in June 1959, linking the Great Lakes to the Atlantic. Fidel Castro took power in Cuba in January. Alaska and Hawaii became the 49th and 50th states. A 116-day steel strike slowed the economy, but the Dow still rose about 16%.

label: First Japanese Cars, Exported to U.S. / U2 Spy Plane Shot Down
summary: The Soviet Union shot down a U-2 spy plane piloted by Francis Gary Powers in May 1960, wrecking a planned summit with Khrushchev. Japanese carmakers such as Toyota and Datsun were just beginning to sell in America, with modest results at first. A recession began, John F. Kennedy won the presidency, and the Dow fell about 9%.

label: The Berlin Wall -- Built / Bay of Pigs -- Debacle
summary: In April 1961 a CIA-backed invasion of Cuba by exiles failed at the Bay of Pigs within three days. In August East Germany built the Berlin Wall to stop people fleeing to the West. Yuri Gagarin became the first person in space. The economy recovered, and the Dow rose about 19%.

label: The Cuban Missile Crisis / Steel Price Rollback
summary: In April Kennedy forced U.S. Steel to cancel a price increase, and the Dow fell 27% by June in what was called the Kennedy Slide. In October U.S. planes found Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba, and for 13 days the world was close to nuclear war before Khrushchev agreed to remove them. Stocks rallied as the crisis ended.

label: John F. Kennedy Assassinated
summary: President Kennedy was shot in Dallas on November 22, 1963. The Dow fell nearly 3% before the NYSE closed early. When trading resumed after the funeral, stocks rose about 4.5%, and the Dow ended the year up about 17%. Martin Luther King Jr. gave his "I Have a Dream" speech in August.

label: Vietnam War Begins -- Gulf of Tonkin Resolution
summary: After reported clashes between U.S. destroyers and North Vietnamese boats, Congress passed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution in August 1964, giving President Johnson broad power to wage war in Vietnam. The Civil Rights Act outlawed discrimination, and a large tax cut passed. The Dow rose about 15%.

label: The Great Inflation -- Begins
summary: Spending on both the Vietnam War and Johnson's Great Society programs, with no tax increase, pushed the economy past full capacity. Inflation began rising from about 1.5% toward double digits over the next 15 years. The Dow came close to 1,000 in early 1966, a level it would struggle to hold for 16 years.

label: Medicare -- Begins / U.S. Bombs North Vietnam -- First Time
summary: Medicare, signed into law in 1965, began paying hospital bills for Americans 65 and older in July 1966. U.S. planes bombed fuel depots around Hanoi and Haiphong for the first time. The Fed tightened credit, causing a credit crunch, and the Dow fell about 19% from its February peak near 1,000.

label: The Six Day War
summary: In June 1967 Israel fought Egypt, Syria and Jordan for six days and took the Sinai Peninsula, Gaza, the West Bank, East Jerusalem and the Golan Heights. Arab oil producers tried an embargo that had little effect. In the U.S., the Dow rose about 15% while antiwar protests and urban riots grew.

label: Tet Offensive / R.F. Kennedy & M.L. King -- Assassinated
summary: North Vietnam's Tet Offensive in January 1968 convinced many Americans the war could not be won quickly, and Johnson declined to run again. Martin Luther King Jr. was killed in April and Robert Kennedy in June. Speculation in small stocks peaked, and the NYSE closed on Wednesdays to clear a paperwork backlog.

label: Apollo 11 -- U.S.A. on the Moon
summary: On July 20, 1969, Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed on the Moon. Back on Earth, the Fed raised rates to fight inflation of about 6%, and a recession began at year end. The Dow fell about 15% in 1969 as the go-go stocks of the late 1960s collapsed.

label: U.S. & South Vietnamese Invade Cambodia / Kent State
summary: Nixon sent troops into Cambodia in April 1970. Protests spread to hundreds of campuses, and on May 4 Ohio National Guardsmen killed four students at Kent State. The Dow hit a low near 631 in May, down 36% from 1968. The Penn Central Railroad collapsed in June, then the largest bankruptcy in U.S. history.

label: Wage & Price Controls
summary: On August 15, 1971, Nixon froze wages and prices for 90 days and ended the dollar's convertibility into gold, which brought down the Bretton Woods system. The Dow jumped 32.9 points the next day, a record at the time. Nasdaq, the first electronic stock market, also began trading in 1971.

label: Watergate -- Break-in / Munich Olympics Massacre
summary: Burglars linked to Nixon's reelection campaign were arrested inside the Democratic headquarters at the Watergate in June 1972. At the Munich Olympics, Palestinian militants killed 11 Israeli athletes and coaches. Nixon won a landslide, and in November the Dow closed above 1,000 for the first time.

label: U.S. Involvement in Vietnam -- Ends / Arab Oil Embargo
summary: The Paris Peace Accords in January ended direct U.S. combat in Vietnam. After the Yom Kippur War in October, Arab oil producers cut off oil to the U.S., and the price of oil quadrupled. Inflation and Watergate began the 1973 to 1974 bear market, in which the Dow lost 45%.

label: President Nixon Resigns / ERISA Act -- Signed
summary: Facing impeachment over Watergate, Richard Nixon resigned on August 9, 1974, and Gerald Ford became president. The Employee Retirement Income Security Act set rules for private pensions and created IRAs. The Dow bottomed at 577.60 in December 1974, with inflation above 12%.

label: Saigon -- Falls / May Day -- Ends Fixed Commissions
summary: North Vietnamese troops took Saigon on April 30, 1975, ending the war. On May 1, called May Day on Wall Street, the SEC ended fixed brokerage commissions, which opened the way for discount brokers like Charles Schwab. John Bogle founded Vanguard and the first index fund followed in 1976. The Dow rose about 38%.

label: U.S. Bicentennial / Lockheed Aircraft -- Bribe Scandal
summary: The U.S. celebrated its 200th birthday on July 4, 1976. Senate hearings showed Lockheed had paid bribes to officials in Japan, the Netherlands, Italy and elsewhere to win aircraft orders, leading to the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act in 1977. Jimmy Carter won the presidency, and the Dow ended near 1,000.

label: Panama Canal Treaty -- Control to Panama in 2000
summary: President Carter and Panama's leader Omar Torrijos signed treaties to hand the Panama Canal to Panama on December 31, 1999. The Senate approved them narrowly in 1978. A falling dollar and rising inflation weighed on stocks, and the Dow lost about 17% in 1977.

label: Humphrey-Hawkins -- "Full Employment" Bill
summary: The Humphrey-Hawkins Full Employment Act required the Federal Reserve to pursue both full employment and stable prices, the Fed's dual mandate, and to report to Congress twice a year. The dollar fell so far that in November Carter announced a rescue package. The Dow ended the year down about 3%.

label: Three Mile Island -- Accident / Iran Hostage Crisis
summary: A partial meltdown at the Three Mile Island nuclear plant in Pennsylvania in March 1979 stalled nuclear power in the U.S. Iran's revolution doubled oil prices, and in November militants seized 52 Americans at the U.S. embassy in Tehran. Paul Volcker became Fed chair and began raising interest rates sharply.

label: Iraq Invades Iran -- War / Hunt Brothers Silver Crisis
summary: The Hunt brothers' attempt to corner silver pushed its price near $50 an ounce. When regulators restricted buying, prices crashed and on Silver Thursday in March the brothers could not meet margin calls. Iraq invaded Iran in September, starting an eight-year war. Inflation hit 14%, and Ronald Reagan won the presidency.

label: Tax Cut -- Passed / Space Shuttle / President Reagan -- Shot
summary: John Hinckley shot President Reagan in March 1981, and Reagan recovered. The space shuttle Columbia made its first flight in April. Congress passed the Economic Recovery Tax Act, cutting the top income tax rate from 70% to 50% over time. The prime rate reached 20.5%, and the economy fell into a deep recession.

label: Penn Square Bank -- Closed by Regulators / Falkland Islands War
summary: Penn Square Bank, an Oklahoma lender that had sold bad energy loans to larger banks, was closed in July 1982. Britain retook the Falkland Islands from Argentina. Mexico's debt crisis hit in August. The Dow bottomed near 777 that month and then began a bull market that ran, with interruptions, for 18 years.

label: Terrorist Bombing of U.S. Barracks -- Beirut / Grenada Invasion
summary: A truck bomb destroyed the Marine barracks in Beirut on October 23, 1983, killing 241 U.S. service members. Two days later U.S. forces invaded Grenada. Inflation fell below 4% and the economy grew strongly. The Dow crossed 1,200 and rose about 20%.

label: Run on Continental Bank
summary: Continental Illinois, the seventh-largest U.S. bank, suffered a run by large depositors in May 1984 after losses on loans bought from Penn Square. Regulators guaranteed all its deposits and took it over. The rescue gave rise to the phrase "too big to fail." The Dow slipped about 4%.

label: Gramm-Rudman Act / U.S. Becomes a Debtor Nation
summary: The Gramm-Rudman-Hollings Act set automatic spending cuts to force down large federal deficits. Because of trade deficits, the U.S. owed more to foreigners than they owed it for the first time since 1914. In September the Plaza Accord pushed the dollar lower, and the Dow rose about 28%.

label: Iran-Contra Affair / U.S. Attacks Libya / Chernobyl Accident
summary: In November it came out that the Reagan administration had secretly sold arms to Iran and sent the money to Contra rebels in Nicaragua. U.S. planes bombed Libya in April after a Berlin disco bombing. Reactor 4 at Chernobyl exploded in April. The Tax Reform Act of 1986 passed, and the Dow rose about 23%.

label: Financial Panic / Stock Market Crash / Iraq Attacks USS STARK
summary: On Black Monday, October 19, 1987, the Dow fell 508 points, or 22.6%, still the largest one-day percentage drop in its history. Computer-driven portfolio insurance selling made it worse. The Fed, under new chair Alan Greenspan, promised to supply cash. In May an Iraqi jet had mistakenly hit the frigate USS Stark, killing 37 sailors.

label: Terrorists Bomb N.Y. Bound Airliner -- Lockerbie, Scotland
summary: A bomb destroyed Pan Am Flight 103 over Lockerbie, Scotland, on December 21, 1988, killing 270 people. A Libyan intelligence officer was later convicted. The NYSE added trading curbs known as circuit breakers after the 1987 crash. The Dow recovered about 12%.

label: The Berlin Wall -- Opens / U.S. Invades Panama
summary: On November 9, 1989, East German guards opened the Berlin Wall, and communist governments across Eastern Europe fell within months. In December U.S. forces invaded Panama and removed Manuel Noriega. The savings and loan bailout began, and the Dow rose about 27%.

label: Iraq Invades Kuwait / German Unification
summary: Iraq invaded Kuwait in August 1990, and oil prices doubled. The U.S. began moving troops to Saudi Arabia, and a recession began. The Dow fell about 21% from July to October. East and West Germany were formally reunited on October 3.

label: The Gulf War / Soviet Union Collapse
summary: A U.S.-led coalition drove Iraq out of Kuwait in a war that began in January and ended in February 1991. Stocks soared on the first night of the air war. In August a coup against Gorbachev failed, and in December the Soviet Union dissolved. The Dow passed 3,000 and rose about 20%.

label: The Cold War -- Ends / Civil War in Bosnia
summary: Presidents Bush and Yeltsin formally declared the Cold War over in February 1992. Yugoslavia broke apart, and war in Bosnia brought the siege of Sarajevo and ethnic cleansing. Britain left Europe's exchange rate system on Black Wednesday. Bill Clinton won the presidency, and the Dow rose about 4%.

label: Russian Revolt / World Trade Center -- Bombed
summary: A truck bomb in the World Trade Center garage in February 1993 killed six people and injured more than 1,000. In Moscow, a standoff between Yeltsin and parliament ended in October when tanks shelled the parliament building. Congress passed a deficit reduction plan, interest rates fell, and the Dow rose about 14%.

label: Orange County Bankruptcy / NAFTA Instituted
summary: NAFTA took effect in January 1994, creating a free trade zone with Canada and Mexico. The Fed doubled short-term rates in a year, causing a bond market rout. Orange County, California lost $1.6 billion on interest rate bets and went bankrupt in December. Mexico's peso collapsed, and the Dow gained about 2%.

label: Oklahoma City -- Murrah Federal Building, Bombed
summary: On April 19, 1995, Timothy McVeigh's truck bomb destroyed the Murrah Federal Building in Oklahoma City, killing 168 people. Netscape's stock market debut in August launched the internet boom. The Dow passed 4,000 and 5,000 and rose about 33%.

label: Alan Greenspan's "Irrational Exuberance" Speech
summary: In a December 1996 speech, Fed chair Alan Greenspan asked how we would know when "irrational exuberance" had pushed asset prices too high. Markets around the world fell the next morning but soon recovered. The Dow passed 6,000 and rose about 26%.

label: Asian Currency Crisis / Hong Kong & Global Stock Market Rout
summary: Thailand's currency collapsed in July 1997, and the crisis spread to Indonesia, South Korea and Malaysia. Hong Kong stocks plunged in October. On October 27 the Dow fell 554 points, or 7.2%, and the first circuit breakers halted trading. It rebounded the next day and rose about 23% for the year.

label: U.S. Intervenes to Support The Yen / African Embassies Bombed
summary: In June 1998 the U.S. joined Japan in buying yen to stop its slide. Al-Qaeda bombed the U.S. embassies in Kenya and Tanzania in August, killing 224 people. Russia defaulted and the hedge fund Long-Term Capital Management collapsed, so the Fed organized a rescue and cut rates three times. The Dow still rose about 16%.

label: NATO Bombs Serbia / Y2K -- Millenium Scare / Columbine
summary: NATO bombed Serbia for 78 days to end the campaign against ethnic Albanians in Kosovo. Two students killed 13 people at Columbine High School in April. Companies spent billions fixing the Y2K bug in old computer code. The Dow closed above 10,000 in March and 11,000 in May as dot-com stocks surged.

label: Bush - Gore Election Crisis / Terrorist Attack on USS COLE
summary: The dot-com bubble burst in March 2000. The Nasdaq peaked and began a fall of 78%. Al-Qaeda bombed the destroyer USS Cole in Yemen in October, killing 17 sailors. The presidential election turned on a Florida recount until the Supreme Court decided Bush v. Gore in December. The Dow fell about 6%.

label: Terrorist Attack on World Trade Center & Pentagon / Enron
summary: On September 11, 2001, al-Qaeda hijackers destroyed the World Trade Center and hit the Pentagon, killing nearly 3,000 people. The NYSE closed for four trading days, and when it reopened the Dow fell 14% in a week. Energy company Enron went bankrupt in December after hiding debts with accounting tricks.

label: War on Terror / Turmoil in the Middle East / Corporate Misconduct
summary: WorldCom's $11 billion accounting fraud followed Enron, and executives at Tyco and others were charged. Congress passed the Sarbanes-Oxley Act to tighten corporate accounting and make chief executives certify their results. Violence rose in Israel and the Palestinian territories. The Dow fell to about 7,286 in October, its lowest in five years.

label: Iraq - Weapons Inspections / War in Iraq
summary: After months of dispute over weapons inspections, the U.S. and its allies invaded Iraq in March 2003, and Baghdad fell in April. No weapons of mass destruction were found. The Fed cut rates to 1%, and Congress cut taxes on dividends and capital gains. Stocks rallied from the start of the war, and the Dow rose about 25%.

label: Global War on Terror
summary: Terrorists bombed commuter trains in Madrid in March 2004, killing 191 people. Fighting in Iraq grew, and the Abu Ghraib prison abuse photos came out. The Fed began raising rates in small steps from 1%. Google went public in August, and the Dow rose about 3%.

label: Record High Oil Prices / Hurricane Katrina
summary: Hurricane Katrina struck the Gulf Coast in August 2005, flooding New Orleans and killing more than 1,800 people. It shut down refineries and offshore oil platforms, and oil prices passed $70 a barrel. Home prices kept rising fast on easy mortgages, and the Dow ended about flat.

label: Housing Decline / Nuclear Weapons - North Korea & Iran
summary: U.S. home prices peaked in mid-2006 and began to fall. North Korea tested its first nuclear weapon in October, and Iran defied UN demands to stop enriching uranium. Ben Bernanke succeeded Greenspan at the Fed. The Dow passed its 2000 high in October and rose about 16%.

label: Subprime Mortgage / Credit Debacle
summary: Defaults on subprime mortgages rose, and in August 2007 BNP Paribas froze funds that held mortgage securities, starting a credit crunch. Britain's Northern Rock suffered the first bank run there in over a century. The Dow peaked at 14,164 on October 9, 2007. It would take about six years to regain that level.

label: Credit Crisis / Financial Institution Failures
summary: Bear Stearns was sold in a Fed-backed rescue in March. In September the government took over Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, Lehman Brothers went bankrupt, and AIG was bailed out. Congress passed the $700 billion TARP rescue. The Dow fell about 34% in 2008, its worst year since 1931.

label: War on Terror / Climate Debate / Healthcare
summary: The Dow hit bottom at 6,547 on March 9, 2009, down 54% from its peak. The Fed bought bonds and Congress passed a $787 billion stimulus. Bank stress tests restored confidence, and stocks rallied about 60% from the low. Obama sent more troops to Afghanistan, the Copenhagen climate summit stalled, and the health care fight dominated Congress.

label: Gulf Oil Spill / European Union Crisis / Massive Debt
summary: BP's Deepwater Horizon rig exploded in April 2010, killing 11 workers and spilling about 4 million barrels of oil into the Gulf of Mexico. Greece needed a bailout, starting Europe's debt crisis. On May 6 the Flash Crash dropped the Dow about 1,000 points in minutes. Congress passed the Dodd-Frank Act and the Affordable Care Act.

label: Debt Ceiling Crisis / U.S. Credit Downgrade
summary: A standoff in Congress over raising the debt ceiling nearly led to a U.S. default. Days after a deal, Standard & Poor's cut the U.S. credit rating from AAA for the first time, and the Dow fell 635 points on August 8. Japan's earthquake and tsunami caused the Fukushima disaster. The Dow still rose about 6%.

label: European Debt / U.S. Fiscal Cliff
summary: In July 2012 European Central Bank president Mario Draghi promised to do "whatever it takes" to save the euro, which calmed the debt crisis. At year end the U.S. faced the fiscal cliff, a set of automatic tax increases and spending cuts, until a last-minute deal. Obama won reelection, and the Dow rose about 7%.

label: Boston Bombing / Government Shutdown / NSA Leaks
summary: Two bombs at the Boston Marathon in April 2013 killed three people and injured hundreds. Edward Snowden leaked documents showing the NSA's mass surveillance programs. The federal government shut down for 16 days in October. The Dow passed its 2007 high in March and rose about 26%, its best year since 1995.

label: Rise of ISIS / Police Protests / Oil Price Decline
summary: ISIS seized Mosul and large parts of Iraq and Syria in June 2014, and U.S. airstrikes began in August. The police shooting of Michael Brown in Ferguson, Missouri, sparked national protests. Oil fell from over $100 to about $55 a barrel by year end. The Fed ended its bond buying, and the Dow passed 18,000.

label: Terror Attacks / Refugee Crisis / China Slowdown / Fed Rate Hike
summary: Terrorists attacked the Charlie Hebdo office in January, and coordinated attacks killed 130 people across Paris in November. Over a million refugees reached Europe. In August China devalued the yuan, and the Dow fell 1,089 points at the open on August 24. In December the Fed raised rates for the first time since 2006. The Dow fell about 2%.

label: Brexit / Cuban Embassy Opened / Elections
summary: British voters chose to leave the European Union in June 2016, and global markets fell sharply for two days before recovering. Obama visited Cuba after embassies reopened the year before. Donald Trump won the presidential election in November, and stocks rallied. The Dow ended the year near 19,763, up about 13%.

label: Dow 20,000 / Manchester Arena Bombing / Bitcoin Mania / Tax Cuts
summary: The Dow crossed 20,000 for the first time in January and kept climbing all year with unusually low volatility. On May 22 a suicide bomber killed 22 people, many of them children and teenagers, as an Ariana Grande concert ended at Manchester Arena, the deadliest attack in Britain since 2005. Two weeks later Grande returned for the One Love Manchester benefit concert, which raised millions for the victims' families. Bitcoin rose from about $1,000 to nearly $20,000 in December, the decade's first great speculative mania, and in December Congress cut the corporate tax rate from 35% to 21%. The Dow ended near 24,719, up about 25%.

label: Volmageddon / US–China Trade War / Christmas Eve Sell-off
summary: On February 5 the VIX volatility index more than doubled in a day, wiping out funds that had bet on calm markets. Washington and Beijing traded escalating tariffs over the year. As the Fed kept raising rates, stocks fell almost 20% in the fourth quarter, with a sharp drop on Christmas Eve. The Dow ended near 23,327, down about 6%, its first losing year since 2008.

label: Fed Reverses Course / Aramco IPO / Trade Truce
summary: The Fed stopped raising rates in January and cut three times by October. A US–China 'phase one' trade deal eased fears late in the year. In December Saudi Aramco listed in Riyadh, the largest IPO in history, valuing the oil company at about $1.7 trillion. The Dow ended near 28,538, up about 22%.

label: COVID-19 Crash / Negative Oil / Fed Rescue
summary: As the pandemic spread, stocks fell more than 30% in about a month, the fastest crash on record, and circuit breakers halted trading four times in March. The Fed cut rates to zero and promised unlimited bond buying, and Congress passed the $2.2 trillion CARES Act. In April US oil futures briefly traded at minus $37 a barrel. Vaccines arrived in December, the Dow crossed 30,000 and ended near 30,606, up about 7%.

label: GameStop Squeeze / Suez Blocked / Inflation Returns
summary: In January small traders on Reddit drove GameStop shares up about seventeenfold in weeks, squeezing hedge funds that had bet against it. In March the container ship Ever Given blocked the Suez Canal for six days. Supply shortages and stimulus pushed US inflation to its highest level in decades by year-end. The Dow ended near 36,338, up about 19%.

label: Russia Invades Ukraine / Fed Hikes / Gilt Crisis / FTX / ChatGPT
summary: Russia invaded Ukraine in February, and European gas prices soared. US inflation peaked at 9.1% in June, and the Fed raised rates faster than at any time since 1980, so stocks and bonds fell together. In Britain a mini-budget set off a gilt crisis and ended Liz Truss's premiership after 49 days. In November the FTX crypto exchange collapsed and OpenAI released ChatGPT. The Dow ended near 33,147, down about 9%.

label: SVB Collapse / Credit Suisse Rescued / AI Boom
summary: In March Silicon Valley Bank failed after a run that took days, the largest US bank failure since 2008, and Swiss authorities forced Credit Suisse into a takeover by UBS. Enthusiasm for artificial intelligence lifted Nvidia past a $1 trillion valuation in May. A handful of giant tech stocks, soon called the Magnificent Seven, drove most of the market's gains. The Dow ended near 37,690, up about 14%.

label: Bitcoin ETFs / Dow 40,000 / Nvidia Joins the Dow / Elections
summary: US regulators approved spot Bitcoin ETFs in January. The Dow crossed 40,000 in May. Nvidia briefly became the world's most valuable company, and in November it replaced Intel in the Dow. Donald Trump won a second term, and stocks rallied. The Dow ended near 42,544, up about 13%.

label: DeepSeek Shock / Liberation Day Tariffs / Gold $4,000
summary: In January the Chinese AI model DeepSeek knocked about $590 billion off Nvidia in one day, the largest single-day loss for any company. On April 2 sweeping 'Liberation Day' tariffs wiped trillions off global markets in two days before a 90-day pause set off a sharp rebound. Gold passed $4,000 an ounce in October as central banks bought heavily. Rate cuts and the AI build-out kept the rally going. The Dow ended the year near 48,063, up about 13%, the S&P 500 about 16% and the Nasdaq about 20%.

label: Dow 50,000 / Iran War & Hormuz Oil Shock / AI Chip Boom
summary: Early in the year the Dow closed above 50,000 for the first time. At the end of February the United States went to war with Iran, which closed the Strait of Hormuz and set off one of the worst oil shortages in decades; US crude jumped from about $67 to more than $110, and stocks bottomed on March 30. A ceasefire on April 8 sent the Dow up more than 1,300 points in a day, though strikes flared again in the summer. Kevin Warsh took over as Fed chair, and chipmakers grew to about a fifth of the S&P 500 as AI spending turned into earnings. By early October the Dow stood near 51,300, up about 7% for the year so far.
